Density and Pressure: Density is mass per unit volume, rho = m / V, in kg/m^3; water is about 1000 kg/m^3 and air about 1.2 kg/m^3. Pressure is force per unit area, P = F / A, measured in pascals (1 Pa = 1 N/m^2). For the same force a smaller area gives a larger pressure, which is why a knife cuts and snowshoes prevent sinking. Atmospheric pressure at sea level is about 1.01 x 10^5 Pa and falls with altitude because there is less air above. A barometer measures atmospheric pressure. Gauge pressure is the pressure above atmospheric pressure and absolute pressure is the total.
Pressure in Fluids: In a fluid at rest pressure increases with depth because of the weight of the fluid above: P = rho g h, where rho is the density of the fluid, g = 9.8 m/s^2 and h is the depth. The pressure at a given depth is the same in all directions and does not depend on the shape of the container. Water pressure rises by about 98,000 Pa (nearly one atmosphere) for every 10 m of depth. The absolute pressure at depth is P = P_atm + rho g h. A mercury barometer balances atmospheric pressure with a column about 0.76 m high.
Pascal's Principle: Pascal's principle says that a pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted undiminished to every part of the fluid and to the walls of its container. A hydraulic lift or press uses this: the pressure under both pistons is the same, so F1 / A1 = F2 / A2 and F2 = F1 x A2 / A1. A small force on a small piston produces a large force on a large piston. Energy is conserved: the small piston moves a long distance and the large piston a short distance, so the work is the same (ideal case). Brakes and car lifts use hydraulics because liquids are almost incompressible.
Buoyancy and Archimedes' Principle: A fluid exerts an upward buoyant force on an object immersed in it. Archimedes' principle says the buoyant force equals the weight of the fluid displaced: F_b = rho_fluid g V_displaced. An object sinks if its average density is greater than the fluid's, floats if it is less, and hovers if equal. A floating object displaces its own weight of fluid, so the fraction submerged equals rho_object / rho_fluid. Steel ships float because their hollow shape displaces a large volume of water. The apparent weight of a submerged object is its weight minus the buoyant force. Hot-air and helium balloons float in air in the same way.
Fluid Flow and Bernoulli's Principle: For an ideal incompressible fluid the flow rate Q = A v is the same everywhere in a pipe, so A1 v1 = A2 v2: the fluid moves faster where the pipe is narrower. Bernoulli's principle is conservation of energy for flowing fluids: P + 1/2 rho v^2 + rho g h is constant along a streamline. In a horizontal pipe, where the speed is higher the pressure is lower. This explains lift on an airplane wing, the spray from an atomizer and why a curveball curves. Torricelli's theorem says water leaves a hole at depth h with speed v = sqrt(2 g h). Real fluids have viscosity, which causes friction and energy loss.
